utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I make one very brief point before proceedings start today? It concerns the matter that arose right at the end of trial yesterday. The transcript of the videotape that was put before the Court by the Prosecutor has the word "Kordic" in there. We believe that the Prosecutor's evidence has already established Mr. Kordic's whereabouts on December the 20th, and that was not in Kiseljak. Actually, it was Colonel Blaskic who addressed the crowd, and I think that there is no dispute about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The reference in the transcript is to Colonel Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It says, "... commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, Colonel Dario Kordic ..." Yes, unfortunately, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone commander was actually Colonel Blaskic, and that was the person who addressed the crowd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're saying that -- what was the word that was used, so I understand the point? Was "Kordic" used or "Blaskic" used?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think the announcer made a mistake. He introduced Mr. Kordic, but it was actually Colonel Blaskic who addressed the crowd. So the word "Kordic" in capitals on the left-hand side there, just before "I hope that you can spend it with your families" should actually say Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well that can be simply amended on our transcripts as we see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're ready to proceed, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let's have the witness then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dan Damon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you got to paragraph 60 on the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In that regard, Your Honour, I will tell the Court, because the Court will certainly know that the subject of the -- the general topic of Kaonik has come up, and the Court has indicated some desire to, can I say, not get bogged down too much further in that material. There are aspects of that in terms of this witness, where Mr. Damon will testify about a meeting with Mr. Kordic about Kaonik, and Mr. Damon was one of the few, if I can use the term, "Western" or "International Community" people who did visit Kaonik. So his perspective is a bit different than the Muslim witnesses who have testified before the Court. Having said that, Your Honour, I would move him through a couple of paragraphs, for instance, on paragraph 72 and 73, by leading him very quickly, but again I think his perspective is different than the testimony the Court has heard before, but we will do it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, is it correct, directing your attention to approximately the middle of May 1993, that you were able to visit an HVO prison camp, if you will, called Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court how you were able to arrange permission, if you will, authorisation, to visit Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one of the occasions when I met Mr. Kordic, we were discussing the threat from the Islamic world to the Croatian people in Bosnia, which Mr. Kordic was keen to impress upon me existed. I asked him for some proof, and he said that there were Islamic fighters imprisoned by the Croats and that we could see them. I suggested that this would be a good idea, and so he arranged, I think, within a very short time, maybe a day or two, for us to be able to visit the camp, which happened to be in Kaonik. I didn't know where it was until we got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me move us back, if I may, to set the scene a bit. Was this conversation with Mr. Kordic at a dinner?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was at one of the dinners that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this dinner?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Eagle's Nest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court a little bit more about the nature of your conversation with Mr. Kordic that evening, before we go ahead to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, like so many politicians in the Croatian region of Bosnia, he believed -- not only politicians, military leaders as well -- he believed that there was an Islamic threat, that the idea of an Islamic state was in the minds of the Muslims living there. Obviously, I tried to suggest that this was perhaps a bit hard to believe, but it was clear that he saw that idea of an Islamic threat in very clear terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make any comment to the effect, something along the lines of, "Those people are dangerous"?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he generalised about Muslims. Whether he used the term "those people," I think the conversation, if I remember, was over several -- well, a couple of hours anyway, but, yes, there was -- in his case, as in so many, there was a tendency to lump together "the Muslims" as being a particular kind of threat. There was a theory abroad in the Croatian community, and particularly amongst the senior politicians, that some kind of Islamic corridor was trying to be created by the Muslims from Turkey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did the subject of Ahmici, the events at Ahmici some days before this dinner also come up in your conversation with Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind that this was a different dinner, but, yes, I can't remember -- I can't distinguish between the two. We did have two. Yes, this was certainly post-Ahmici. I was very, well, upset. If I can just briefly beg the indulgence of the Court, I'd like to set the scene because I think it is quite important. I had during the previous year, in 1991, I had filmed alongside Croatian soldiers when Croatia was being attacked by the Yugoslav People's Army. I was in that region, Zagreb and the Krajina region, for some considerable months, and I developed a strong respect for the bravery of the Croatian soldiers, many of whom were not soldiers; they were people who were brought together very rapidly to deal with the threat. For example, I made a film about a cinematographer, Gordon Lederer, who had no interest in this idea of ethnic purity but who had been killed filming alongside Croatian soldiers because he felt his country's case was not being heard. In so many cases, I believed it was the morale of the Croatian people that enabled them to resist what was an enormous assault. A huge part of one of Europe's largest armies was thrown against Croatia in 1991. As I say, that morale, that morality seemed to be important to their survival, and survive, they did. Then when I game to Central Bosnia in the end of 1992, 1993, I saw exactly the same kind of immorality that I'd seen used against the Croatians being used by them or by people claiming to be representing the Croatian nation in Central Bosnia, and this offended me, not just me. I did feel in a way that this was a disastrous situation for the Croatians to be in. So, perhaps naively, at this dinner, I took Mr. Kordic to one side, I asked for a private meeting with him, just me and a translator, in a side room, and I made it clear that this situation, this incident in Ahmici was a very negative development for the Croatians, apart from the damage that it caused to the Muslims, because it was immoral. There was no political reason for massacring babies a few months old. I suggested to him that since it was clear, at least some of the names of those involved were already known to the U.N. investigators, that the Croatian leadership should help in bringing them to justice and to making sure that justice was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall Mr. Kordic making any response to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was gracious. He said -- he said that there were extremists on all sides, which was a common response whenever one confronted a politician who had power to stop these things and who wasn't able or willing to do so, and met the same response in other parts with other political leaders on all sides. That was it. I mean, there was no -- he didn't make any admission, of course, and -- but at the same time, I don't believe that he went ahead and instigated an investigation or that, indeed, anybody who had the power, and Mr. Kordic certainly had tremendous power in that valley, did anything to find out who were the perpetrators or to make sure that justice was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, after that conversation, whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we ask the witness if Mr. Kordic commented on the morality or immorality, the legality or illegality, of the acts that the witness has just spoken of?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, can you assist the Court with that?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood the question. No, there was no comment on its rightness or wrongness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether, following this conversation, did the interpreter who was with you during this exchange express any view to you about the proposal, if you will, of a Bosnian Croat investigation?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- as we left afterwards, one of the translators commented that really I was barking up the wrong tree because there was quite clearly a policy which was in the hands of the political leadership to exclude all of the Muslims, and that the suggestion that there were just a few perpetrators who were out of control was silly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just following up on that, your proposal or suggestion to Mr. Kordic had been that the Croats, that it would be in their interest to conduct their own investigation, to bring the perpetrators to justice?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two things in my mind. The first, that I've already alluded to, that I genuinely and perhaps naively felt that this was a great disaster for the Croatian spirit, and indeed, as it proved, the project to create an ethnically pure Herceg-Bosna failed, but also, as a journalist, I sort of felt that there -- I really felt that they might want to help me get to the bottom of this atrocity. I had built up a level of trust with the Croatians, coincidentally -- well, in the previous year, the Croatian television in the Republic of Croatia had made a documentary about me because they seemed to think that I was a journalist who had some credibility, so I was hoping that they would enable me to get to the bottom of what was clearly an outrage, and one which did no service whatsoever to the idea of the Croatians defending their own religion and ability to live at peace in their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we go on to Kaonik, just to set the scene on that again, this particular topic had come up in your conversation with Mr. Kordic at dinner, because you said a few moments ago that there was some suggestion by Mr. Kordic that there were outside Muslim soldiers, if you will, who were involved in the fighting in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I would like to emphasise that I believe that to be true. In fact, whether the people that I saw were those fighters is highly questionable, but there were many sources who told us, including Bosnian army sources, who told us that there were indeed Islamic fighters, so-called Afghanis -- although I believe that they were, in fact, from other countries than Afghanistan, they were called Afghanis because they had fought inside Afghanistan at various times or had been trained there -- and so I asked for proof, and Mr. Kordic arranged for me to get it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By going to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: By going to the Kaonik camp, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you went to Kaonik camp on the 14th of May, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the date on the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just, again, to set this dinner conversation in a time frame, how long before, or shortly before, if you will, was this dinner in relation to your visit at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was a very short time. It may have been the following day, or a day after that, that we were able to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Kaonik on the 14th of May, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went up a lane to what looked like an old Yugoslav People's Army barracks or store area surrounded by a fence, and we were taken just to one building, which looked like some sort of storehouse, although it had rooms that were -- looked like purpose-built cells. We were allowed to film in just a couple of these. We saw the Islamic citizens, citizens of Pakistan, Turkey, and I think other countries. We were told there were about a dozen of them; I think we saw about eight, six to eight of them. The conditions were, I thought, very bad. I saw worse in other camps, but they were bad, mostly because there was no hygiene for these people, and that was quite important to them. I remember having a discussion -- we were allowed -- I would like to say we were allowed to talk to these people without the Croatian soldiers being in the cell with us; they were outside. I had a conversation with one of them about the difficulties of practising his religion, because they like to wash before praying, and he said that his religion enabled him simply to wipe his hands on the wall as a gesture of going through the ritual. But it was clearly -- I mean, it was very smelly, it was very dirty, and the conditions were certainly less than any prisoner of war should have been kept in, or indeed any prisoner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Kaonik, to your observation, an HVO military prison?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was certainly in the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the guards or soldiers that you saw there in HVO uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any -- can you make any observations or did you have any impressions about the attitude of the HVO soldiers or commanders at Kaonik about your presence there?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they weren't very happy about it, I think quite understandably. They were not that used to having journalists poking their noses and cameras into prisons. I mean, as I said, I went into worse. There were other installations where certainly there was a lot more to hide, but I guess it was a combination of having been free to operate without scrutiny up until then, and also the general feeling which prevailed because under the old communist system, there would be no form of journalism which would enable anybody to go into such a place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Kaonik on that morning, was there some communication or information that Dario Kordic had authorised you to come into the camp?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the translator who got the permission had no doubt where it had come from. There may even have been a bit of paper, although I didn't look at it closely, but I think there certainly was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether there was any indication that the HVO officials at the camp were unhappy particularly at Mr. Kordic for having authorised you to come there?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some discomfiture. A conversation went on at the gate, but I didn't understand it. It was clear that they were not happy we were there, but they had superior orders, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before we close on that, did it come to your attention or can you share with the Court any knowledge you have: Were these prisoners subsequently exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them exchanged a few days later, in the centre of Zenica, and it was an exchange supervised by the British army. We were allowed to observe it from our vehicles for a short period, and then one of the Islamic -- I say "Islamic," one of -- there was a separate -- there was quite clearly a separate group in charge of this, other than the Bosnian army, of this exchange in Zenica. One of them pointed an anti-aircraft gun directly at our vehicle, and a British army soldier stuck his head inside the cab and said something in Anglo-Saxon to the effect that we should leave. It seemed like a good idea at the time. I went, actually -- again, in my naive and offended way, I went to the police chief in Zenica, the Bosnian police chief, and said, "What are you doing about these people running around your city with anti-aircraft guns?" And he shrugged his shoulders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I want to direct your attention to another matter. Did you come to know, around this time, or through your travels in Central Bosnia, about a building or facility that was known or referred to as the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was a wooden building quite close to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to have any information about who occupied or used that building?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was information -- I have to say by hearsay and rumour, but this was said to be the base of the hard-line soldiers, paramilitaries, who were responsible for what had gone on in Ahmici, although it was occupied by the military before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have occasion sometime after Ahmici to go to the Bungalow and speak with some of these people?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the same spirit of naivety I went to them and asked what was going on. Again, I made this somewhat romantic point about having been in ditches side by side with Croatian soldiers during 1991 and that this was not the way I expected them to behave. I was given the story about the village of Cajdras, up in the hills behind Ahmici, where there was said to be atrocities against Croats, as if this was some kind of explanation for what had gone on in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you that very directly: Did you ask them, did you put the question to them as why had Ahmici happened, or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what answer did you get?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Cajdras was the reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went to Cajdras. We went the long way round through Zenica, which was the easy way of crossing the line, and although subsequently we did cross the line directly to Cajdras from different occasions, but on this occasion we went round the long way to investigate, and we found that the men had been arrested, indeed. We later saw those men in prison in Zenica when the Red Cross was there. But the women and the families, the children and the older people, were in reasonably good shape, and I met the priest also who was responsible for their welfare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he seem to have free access to move about the area?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. We spoke to him briefly about the difficulties, and of course he made it clear that they were concerned for the future. But I did ask him directly: "Are you being harassed?" And he said, "No, not at this time." There had been, up in remote Croatian households away from the village, there had been some trouble, but not inside the village itself, and certainly it wasn't a massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before moving on in the chronology, is it fair to say, Mr. Damon, that by this point in time -- we're now into May of 1993 -- that you had travelled fairly extensively in Central Bosnia, including the areas of Busovaca, Nadioci, and Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just share with the Court -- I don't want to lead you through this, but just share with the Court your views, based on having interviewed a number of people, in terms of the attitudes and the statements of viewpoint, if you will, that you saw between the various ethnic groups about their coexistence?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a policy, and it was clear that it was being effected, to purify the region. Once the idea of purification had begun, then it was a military campaign that was engaged in to clear out the Muslims. It was first begun in October of 1992. It -- I think at the highest level there was some truce negotiated then, but through the spring of 1993, it was gradually built up until in April, the atrocities against the Muslims began in and around Vitez, and in Ahmici subsequently, and elsewhere. And there was an attitude, and one met this in many parts of Herzegovina, that the Muslims were not to be trusted and that they had to be cleared out. I remember meeting villagers further down towards Mostar, villages that had been under shell fire from the Serb side earlier in the war but who said they would rather live with the Serbs than the Muslims, who had never shelled them. There was a great deal of racial ill feeling stirred up, I believe. I think there is plenty of proof that it was part of a political plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, your answer has implied the answer to this, but you started out your answer a moment ago by saying there was a policy. With which of the ethnic groups were you identifying this policy?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a plan by some Croatian politicians to create a state of Herceg-Bosna that would be annexed to Croatia. I saw a piece of paper which contained this plan and was signed by various senior Croatian politicians. I was shown a photocopy of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give any particular date as to when you saw this document, or the date of the document?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was dated October 1991. I don't remember when I saw it. I have a feeling I've still got it somewhere in my papers. I've been trying to track it down. I haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, returning to this other topic, I'd like you to go further, if you can, with the Court and tell the Court about any differences of opinion or attitude you saw in this respect, between the Croats on the one side and the Muslims on the other, in terms of mutual coexistence?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't want to be too romantic about it. There clearly were excesses and outrages carried out by all sides. I saw later in the year of 1993 or in the early part of '94, I saw a Catholic Church up in the hills, which had been above Konjic, which had been trashed apparently by Muslims, so these things happened. But in terms of the initiation of this spirit of aggression and ethnic purity, this was evidently a Croatian plan. I spoke, for example, in Mostar to some teenaged boys. In fact, I made a short documentary about them, and they said quite clearly -- these were Muslims on the east bank of Mostar who said quite clearly, "We would like to live with them, but I don't think they want to live with us." Perhaps one of the understatements of the century, to be honest, but that was quite clearly the mood. You, of course, would find -- I also met Muslim soldiers injured, amputees, in the hospital in Zenica, who had been flown in from the Muslim areas of eastern Bosnia, who were quite clearly anti-Christian. One might suppose that their experiences had radicalised them. But in terms of a plan, a policy to separate the different coreligionists, that was a Croatian plan, I'm afraid to say, which is a tragedy because, in fact, the similarities between these people were much more important and valuable than the differences between them. But a certain type of politician chose to stir up trouble.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move on, then, to your trips to Cajdras. You spoke about that already. Did you then make a second visit, with a Bosnian official, to Cajdras?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were in Zenica a few days later. Again, I can't specifically remember the date, but it would be on the tape. And I'm afraid I have to admit in an exercise, to some extent, of news management we met the vice-president of Bosnia, Ejub Ganic, who I knew already from having interviewed him in Sarajevo, and I suggested that he should go to Cajdras. Two reasons: Firstly, I thought it would demonstrate that indeed nothing had happened in Cajdras, but also I felt that it was important that he should see what was going on, that it was easy for politicians in Sarajevo to be isolated from what was going on in the countryside. He accepted our suggestion, and he drove up to Cajdras to meet the priest. Also one of the women there who was quite outspoken, who had previously given me an interview, expressed an opinion which I heard far too rarely, which was that she was as worried for women with children on the other side of the divide as she was for her own people. She was a Croat, and she said that she was worried about the women and children on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just by point of reference, was the Catholic priest Father Stjepan?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the video booth, if we could play, what's described for their reference as, video 1064, 1-0-6-4, which, for the record, has been marked as Prosecution Exhibit 930.1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The booth doesn't have the cassette.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There may be a misnumbering. Check 1089. I believe the exhibit number is correct, Your Honour, 930.1, but the video number may have been misstated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, is this the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following your trip, your visit to Cajdras then, can you tell the Court whether you developed a conclusion as to the truth of the information that the soldiers at the Bungalow had given you as an explanation for Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it never would have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I think we are venturing into matters of opinion rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe we've covered paragraph 87. Now, in approximately mid May of 1993, did you have occasion, Mr. Damon, to videotape, you or your crew, a meeting or series of meetings in Bosnia involving President Tudjman, Mate Boban, and others, at a meeting with Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the video booth can please play what has been marked as Exhibit 936.1, which is the first tape marked "1108." There are two 1108s because there's two portions, but it should be the first of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is a second tape, which is Exhibit 936.2 and which is also marked 1108 and which follows on from this tape. If we could play that, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, you expressed earlier that you became convinced that there was a Croat policy or a plan to ethnically cleanse Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, again, we're now venturing into areas which we are going to have to decide. While we can hear what the witness saw and heard and his reports of those things, his opinions on matters which we are going to have to decide are, with due respect to him, as far as these proceedings are concerned, irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it come to your attention during the events in the Lasva Valley in May -- excuse me, April of 1993 that there had been a series of attacks all launched roughly the same day?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were certainly a series of attacks all the way along the valley over a number of days. I believe that they started on one particular day, but there was no doubt that these were coordinated attacks aimed at the Muslims specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether it had come to your attention some days before Ahmici, for instance, whether there had been some HVO ultimatum issued?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I must object to that, Your Honour, on the grounds of hearsay. Apparently, according to the offer of proof, we have apparently what appears to be a report from an unidentified member of the opposing force as to what an unidentified member of the other force supposedly said. So that's at least two stages of hearsay and probably more. So we object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you better establish the basis for this, and we'll decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, Mr. Damon, the source of your information about this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a briefing given to me in Tuzla by the spokesperson for the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this in the course of your journalistic coverage?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was interviewing him, and he told me that this ultimatum had been given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the nature of the ultimatum in terms of what will happen if something else doesn't happen, in that sense?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no "what would happen." He just said that they had been told to hand over all of their weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your time in Central Bosnia, Mr. Damon, did you ultimately come away from your experience with a view towards what role Dario Kordic played in the events there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Again that's precisely the point, indeed, the very point that we're going to have to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I don't think -- it's not opinion. It's simply that this is a man who travelled and dealt in this area extensively. So I didn't mean it to be speculation, but I understand the Court's ruling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me close with this then, Mr. Damon, if I can. Based on observations, you saw Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic on a number of occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your observations, did you see evidenced to you the nature of the relationship between Mr. Kordic and Mr. Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Blaskic was a military man, former Yugoslav People's Army, and he was operating as the military commander for the region at a certain level. There was no doubt in my mind that his superior was Dario Kordic. Of course, as a soldier from the former Yugoslav People's Army, he would undoubtedly look for political direction, and that political direction came from Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers. Cross-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, good morning. My name is Steve Sayers and I represent Dario Kordic. I would just like to reiterate what Mr. Scott said. Since we speak the same language, if we speak too quickly, the interpreters get justifiably angry with us, and so it creates an unclear record. If you would just have a pause between the question and the answer, I'd appreciate it. Thank you. Did you ever see Dario Kordic give any kind of a military order to Colonel Blaskic in any of the meetings that you had, sir?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, you worked as a freelance journalist in 1992 and 1993 throughout -- and 1994, for that matter, in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked for SkyNews and other services, and I believe that SkyNews is a satellite television service that was part of the media empire built up by the late Rupert Murdoch; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's not late; he's just divorced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I stand duly corrected. Your territory or beat, if you like, covered the whole of Eastern Europe; right?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, and elsewhere, but mostly Eastern Europe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you do not speak any Croatian, do you? I understand that --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think what you mean to say is that at the time, I didn't speak Croatian. I should make it clear that I have spent the last year learning this language as part of a course that I'm engaged in, but at the time, no, I didn't speak it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You relied a lot upon your translators?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Closely, yes. After a period, one gets a feeling for what's going on. The Croatian language is not as remote as some others that I've learned. I learned Hungarian, for example, which has no very great connection with Indo-European languages. I could understand more of what was going on in Croatian, but, yes, you're quite right, I relied on the translators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you, in your vocation and job, have been trained to differentiate hard facts from rumours, stories, and so-called conventional thinking; right?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know how to distinguish what people have seen with their own eyes and ears with from what they've not, what are merely stories and rumours; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: One tries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's important to you, indeed, it's crucial to your reporting, to your reputation, and, of course, your livelihood to make sure that your reporting is factually accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: One tries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In doing so, it's important to make sure that when you're reporting events, you know who they involve, where they occurred, what was involved; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As much as possible. There should be no deceit. Of course, mistakes are possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. On that subject, would you agree with me that you found yourself in the middle of a chaotic, confusing civil war where there was an intense use of misinformation and disinformation on all sides?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't accept the word "confusing." It was confusing to a great many. I had been there for quite a long time. I was perhaps less confused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, nonetheless, it would be fair to say that there was routine use of disinformation and misinformation in the media sources used by all the participants in that civil war, Bosnian Serb, Bosnian Muslim, and Bosnian Croat; that's a fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I myself was a victim of this. I mentioned to the Court that my reports being available on the satellite were taken down and recorded by all of the different local television stations and translations made of my commentary, and on several occasions, it became clear to me that the translations had been used for disinformation, had been made inaccurately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You travelled to the area of Gornji Vakuf, or Skopje, as it's otherwise known, in the summer of 1992, and you actually found the Muslim forces and the Croat forces cooperating there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, just to the north, the Muslims and the Croats were cooperating in fending off the Serb assault; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to lay the foundation -- and I won't spend more than a minute or so on this -- to give the Trial Chamber a sense of what was going on in Central Bosnia in 1992 and early 1993, wouldn't it be fair to say that there was an intensive Bosnian Serb offensive from the west, from the east, and also from the north?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that resulted in the influx, if you will, of the large numbers of refugees into Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the subject of the political organisations that you have described, you actually met Mr. Mate Boban in person; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to interview twice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've seen from the videotapes that you've put in evidence before the Trial Chamber that Mr. Boban was the Croat spokesman at the negotiations that occurred in Medjugorje in the latter half of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Kordic never attended any of those negotiations, did he?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Boban was actually the president of an entity known as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't know that. I knew him to be the president, the leader, of the Croatian Democratic Union party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what positions within that entity that I've just mentioned Mr. Kordic occupied, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, we were told he was number two to Mr. Boban in the HDZ. As you've heard from the tape --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, I said the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, not the HDZ. What I wanted to ask you was: What was Mr. Kordic's position in that entity, if you know? And if you don't, that's fine too.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that he was number two to Mr. Boban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many vice-presidents were there of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Bozo Rajic was also a vice-president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that he was a senior figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning now to the HDZ, do you know what that refers to, those initials?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the political party. Do you know who the president of the political party was at the time that you were in Central Bosnia, sir?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the local --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, the national HDZ.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And is the same true on the local level, in Busovaca and Vitez, for example? Do you know who the president of the local HDZ --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know any of the details of the structure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that on a national level, the HDZ BiH actually had five vice-presidents, of whom Mr. Kordic was one?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that in your meetings with Mr. Boban, you found him to be a forceful personality?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not especially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find Mr. Kordic to be a forceful personality?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't think any opinion that I formed has any political relevance, if I may put it like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You met him -- Mr. Kordic, that is -- about three or four times?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you always found him a gracious host during the meetings that --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was certainly polite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He always went out of his way to help you, did he not?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, would it be fair to say that he actually facilitated your access and your press colleagues' access to go, insofar as it was within his power to arrange, wherever you wanted?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak for my other colleagues, but in my case, yes, he was helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He never placed any limits on what you could see, did he?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He personally didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or to whom you could speak?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, when you approached him with requests for assistance in a variety of contexts, he did his best to assist you, did he?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. He was a powerful man, and he was able to use that power to our benefit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that the Croat people living in Bosnia and Herzegovina were in a rather small minority, approximately 17,4 per cent of the entire population?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, that was the figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions on the local political structures that I haven't already covered. Did you ever have occasion to speak with the head of the civilian HVO government in Busovaca, Mr. Zoran Maric?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember meeting him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you ever remember meeting the commander of the HVO brigade stationed in Busovaca, Mr. Dusko Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name sound familiar at all?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Maric's name, I take it, is unfamiliar too?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Maric's is a name that I am familiar with, but I met a lot of commanders, and I'm afraid the names don't stick.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with the head of the civilian HVO government in Vitez, Mr. Ivica Santic?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name rings more of a bell, but I couldn't tell you how and when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You were asked some questions regarding a -- what I believe is a singular sighting of a truck carrying HV plates, or -- not HV plates, but license plates from the state of Croatia. Throughout all of the years that you were a reporter, travelling around, speaking to people, and seeing what was going on in your area of reportage, it's true, is it not, that you only ever saw one such truck?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only ever noticed the one truck, for the reason that I suggested, that it nearly hit us. You said "in speaking to people," no, in speaking to people, one heard widely of the connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'm asking you, sir, what you saw with your own eyes.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you said both things, and I never -- I don't recollect seeing more than the one truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was, I believe, sir, a few kilometres inside the southwestern border between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at the town of Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few kilometres, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's in southwest Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know what the identity was of the people that were in that truck, do you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You didn't notice any insignia that they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you didn't even notice whether there were any people in the truck, apart from the driver, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was concentrating on the front of the truck and not the people inside it, I have to ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've already informed the Trial Chamber that you never saw any troops, regular troops from the Republic of Croatia, in the town of Busovaca. The same is true, actually, for the entire Lasva Valley, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Lepenica valley, the so-called Kiseljak valley, to the southeast?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recollect, that's true, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to the HVO commander that you referred to in 1994, Ante Roso?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the troop exercises that were shown on one of the videotapes that was run in the courtroom, you did not, yourself, actually see the troop exercises, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember testifying before this Tribunal in the case against Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever have the opportunity to meet any of the notorious paramilitary unit leaders that you referred to in that case?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I refer to? What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me lay a foundation for that term. There were a number of paramilitary units that you saw throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, on both sides, I suppose --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. On the Croatian side, the only one I met that was described as a paramilitary unit was the Jokers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never met any of the leaders who were the most notorious? I believe that's what you said. On page 1284 of Aleksovski, you said, "I did not meet any of the paramilitary leaders who were the most notorious."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be proper if the transcript were shown to the witness, if he's going to question him about it?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't dispute it. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he doesn't remember. I don't think it's going to assist us.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't dispute that I said that, and it's true. I never knowingly met any of those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know who the leader of the Jokers unit that you've described --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, turning to fighting that broke out in the spring of 1993, it's true, is it not, that you had noticed, significantly prior to that date, increasing tensions between the HVO and the TO forces, the Territorial Defence forces?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I described earlier the occasion in October when we had to pass through a battle zone, and we were interviewing to Muslims on a checkpoint close to the school which became the British base, and we were -- we began to be fired at by what I assumed to be Croatian forces -- I mean, it wouldn't have been -- I guess it would not have been Muslims, since we were interviewing the Muslims at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Muslim forces had actually set up a checkpoint fairly a close to the BritBat headquarters at Nova Bila, and the fighting broke out as you were interviewing the people manning the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't that fighting broke out; we came under fire. We were at the time interviewing, in fact, unarmed Muslims at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so we have our terminology straight, the forces that later became known as the ABiH were actually referred to in the spring of 1993 as the TO or the Territorial Defence, and they actually wore TO patches; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the change took place, I can't remember, but yes, they were certainly -- in the early part of the war, they were known as TO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be fair to say -- and I don't think that there is any dispute about this -- that it was routine to see people operating in their daily activities dressed in camouflage uniforms, on both sides --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Muslims and Croats? In fact, you would even see secretaries, lady secretaries, dressed in camouflage uniforms as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wearing high heels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Camouflage and high heels, all right. It would be fair to say that there wasn't a -- how shall we say -- a wide degree of uniformity in the attire that you generally saw? You saw bits and pieces of camouflage --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amongst many, but there of course were many units who were properly attired and disciplined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was also common in your experience in that time, 1993, to see people wearing military insignia, and even military police insignia, who to you had obviously never had a day's training in their life? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the military police, but certainly, yes, there were people wearing military insignia who didn't look as though they'd -- well, it may have been some years since they were conscripted into the Yugoslav People's Army, put it like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to turn to the testimony that you gave regarding the briefing you received from the commander of the Muslim troops, I believe in Zenica, was it prior to --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tuzla? You never saw any ultimatum or order signed by anybody, yourself, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. He showed me a map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He pointed out the areas on the map where this demand had been made, he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He said. So the only thing that you know about such a demand, if it had ever been made, was what this military commander from the Muslim forces told you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you met Colonel Blaskic on several occasions in Vitez, at his headquarters in the Hotel Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was actually extremely close to your -- the base of operations that you had set up, at least in the first part of 1993, which I believe was right next door to the BritBat base at Nova Bila?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early part of '93, no. We were still, I think, in the cafe near the convent, near to Kiseljak. But, yes, we did set up -- after Ahmici, we set up in a house near BritBat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that subject, Mr. Damon, as you travelled north along that road from the accommodations that you'd set up above the cafe, you actually arrived at a major checkpoint at the village of Kacuni; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, indeed, throughout the time --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just on the bridge we're referring to, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout the time that you were in that part of Central Bosnia, from January until 1995, if you like, the area of road between Kacuni and Bilalovac, about three or four kilometres to the south, that was actually controlled exclusively by Muslim forces, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recollect, the first Muslim checkpoint was some way down towards Zenica. I don't -- I don't know any further. I mean, I can tell you what the British army told me, but I don't think you want to hear that, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you knew that between Kacuni and Bilalovac, that was Muslim territory; right?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as I say, my recollection is there was a kind of no-man's land and that the first Muslim checkpoint was some way towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the silos detention facility where significant numbers of Croats were being held prisoner in the early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The silos I visited were in Tarcin, and there were Serbs being kept there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, but that was much further to the south. All right. Now, you've described Colonel Blaskic as the military commander of all of the HVO military forces in Central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how he was described to me, and that appeared to be his position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And initially, whenever you found that you needed permission to do various things, to travel to places, to meet people, he was the soldier to go to arrange that, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some period, that's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also described going down to Kiseljak to obtain permission to film in the area of the Kiseljak valley?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember -- is this -- you're referring to a period earlier in the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you actually met the Kiseljak police chief, Vinko --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Lucic?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We went to his house once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, I'm interrupting you simply to remind you that in general terms, you do not need to remind a witness every time about what he said previously during the interrogation in chief, because in the Trial Chamber, we have taken note of that. We would ask that you not have the witness repeat, moving things forward more quickly. You know, time is very precious here at the International Criminal Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, why not go simply to the point? "When you were filming in Kiseljak, did you do this or that," or whatever it is you want to ask. No need to go over what you said before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were filming in Kiseljak, you went to the chief of police, Vinko Lukic, to request permission to do that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we felt there was likely to be some objection to what we wanted to do. In general, in the early part of the war, we could move around -- well, freely, subject to military dangers. But in terms of getting permissions, gradually we built up an understanding of who were the right people to go to for different jobs, depending on the sensitivity of those jobs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it was a sensitive area, he told you to get in touch with Colonel Blaskic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and beyond Colonel Blaskic, for especially sensitive, then it was made clear that it was a political command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've given some testimony to the effect that Mr. -- you've described Colonel Blaskic as following superior orders from someone. Did Colonel Blaskic ever tell you that he was following superior orders from some identified person?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me. I don't speak his -- didn't speak his language then. I'm trying to recollect the tone of conversations that were held. The translator, in particular, that I was using was not simply a translator in the sense that he was simultaneously saying and responding; he was part of the team. He had been a senior Yugoslav journalist in Vojvodina, so he had plenty of his own conversations and then would fill me in as to what was said. I don't specifically recollect a word-for-word conversation, but I do know that that translator told me on several occasions what the hierarchy was in the valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was -- sorry. It was as you described, that Colonel Blaskic was the military commander, there was a political leadership, and Dario Kordic was the senior political figure in the valley.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Colonel Blaskic's superior officer?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I ever asked that, I don't recollect, but it was clearly out of the area anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you've never met or spoken with Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I may have attended a press conference once at which he was a participant, but I don't remember specifically ever speaking to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the subject of Colonel Blaskic, you found him a disciplined, professional soldier; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In command of a well-organised and well-disciplined military in the region; yes?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was in command of troops that were disciplined and did what he ordered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, in the meetings that were held between Colonel Blaskic and Colonel Stewart which you've related, Colonel Blaskic admitted, for example, that the village of Ahmici was broadly within his area of responsibility; yes?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also said that he was responsible for the military events that occurred on April the 16th, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He accepted responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he denied and specifically denied that he had ever ordered any massacre at Ahmici, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to ask Colonel Stewart for the details of the conversation, but that's what Colonel Stewart told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no evidence to offer the Trial Chamber that Colonel Blaskic actually ordered any kind of a massacre at Ahmici, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, the same is true of Mr. Kordic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, yes, it is. I think it's the subsequent events that should engage the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the village of Ahmici, you actually saw ammunition boxes with Middle Eastern script on them, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Chinese.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you see some from Middle Eastern countries too?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you not see ammunition boxes with Middle Eastern script on them in the village of Ahmici when you visited that village in April and May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. No, I don't remember that. I remember seeing Chinese writing on munitions above Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just turn to page 1287 of your testimony in the Aleksovski case, where you said, lines 5 through 7: A We saw various types of ammunition all over that theatre, of course, with lots of different sources, some apparently from Middle Eastern countries, some from Cyrillic speaking countries, and some from China.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. But you mentioned Ahmici. I don't remember identifying any ammunition in Ahmici. Yes, we did certainly see Middle Eastern weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just one question regarding the minaret that you saw had toppled down. Did you notice at any time when you were present in April or May of 1993 any graffiti on that minaret, sir?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that 12 Croats had been massacred at the village of Dusina on January the 26th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why do you ask the witness that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Why, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Because I believe Mr. Damon has stated that he was unaware that there were any massacres of Croats by Muslim forces in the Lasva Valley. At least that's what I thought he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of that or not, Mr. Damon?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. I did not say that there were not atrocities carried out on all sides. I believe there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness said was that there were excesses on both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, you said that you were in Tuzla when the fighting broke out. Were you aware of the events that immediately preceded the outbreak of fighting in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If, by this, you mean that there had been a slow buildup, no. I was aware from my reports and from conversations with my BBC colleague that there had been a sudden escalation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You have no personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so. Not so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I'll move on. Turning to the conversations that you had with Mr. Kordic, you have described Mr. Kordic expressing some concerns to you, over the course of a dinner that lasted some hours, I believe, about a threat from Mujahedin from various Middle Eastern countries like Libya, Iran, Algeria, fighting on behalf of the TO, the Territorial Defence, in Central Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember those specific countries being mentioned, but, yes, the idea of there being Islamic fighters was discussed as a confirmation of his fear that an Islamic state was being created.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a concern that you had heard articulated several times before from numerous people; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd heard it from a senior commander in Prozor, who drew me a map demonstrating how this Islamic threat was building up, and at a lower level -- well, all over Bosnia, you would hear similar theories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So this was not an individual perspective that was in any way a surprise for you to hear or unusual for a Croat, for example, to express?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, it was a surprise to me because Dario Kordic, as I understand it, was a journalist at some stage earlier in his career, I knew him to be an intelligent man, and, therefore, to hear this conspiracy theory based on an extreme racial view from somebody who had this background was a surprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kordic express extreme racial views to you during the course of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He expressed the view that there was an attempted Islamic takeover and that the Muslims were dangerous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, he expressed views that he was concerned about Mujahedin fighters in Central Bosnia and you asked him to prove that, and in order to do so, he facilitated a visit to the military prison at Kaonik; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that wasn't the only expression of his fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did Mr. Kordic go about arranging that visit to Kaonik? You just don't know really, do you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know if Mr. Kordic delegated that task to someone else, do you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, it's the time we usually take a break. When you come to a convenient moment -- is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Perfectly convenient, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now until half past eleven. You are, I hope, moving on with your cross-examination, or you seem to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I am, I'm delighted to report, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, I'll try to be through with you in about 20 minutes, if that's convenient. You didn't make any personal notes or memoranda to the file about your conversations with Mr. Kordic in May of 1993, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No contemporaneous notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's true that you never actually discussed with Mr. Kordic the chain of military command in Central Bosnia on the HVO side, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the same goes for Colonel Blaskic, too?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I discuss the military command with Colonel Blaskic? I think I probably did discuss dispositions with him. I seem to remember him also showing me various dispositions on a map as to where different troops lay, and front lines, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you never actually discussed the subject of the formal chain of command, who reported to whom, in what context, or anything like that, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with him, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the dinners that you've described with Mr. Kordic, I believe Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kostroman were also present at those dinners; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Colonel Blaskic being present at either of them, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Who else was present at them, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I can't give you names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from my translators, and I don't choose to give those names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on May the 13th, you asked for a private aside, as you've said, with Mr. Kordic, and he didn't object to that, did he?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was perfectly willing to speak to you on the subjects that you wanted to address with him?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave some testimony regarding some passports issued to your interpreters. Do you know to whom Mr. Kordic spoke in order to arrange the issuance of those documents?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You simply don't know anything about the process which led to -- or other than your request to Mr. Kordic, but you don't know anything about the process by which the documents were issued?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Not -- not my request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've stated that everybody referred to Mr. Kordic's headquarters as "the Eagle's Nest." He never referred to it by that name, did he, to you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people in uniform that you described being in attendance at this location, you don't remember seeing any particular patches or identifying marks regarding the units to which these people belonged, do you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, there were some military police around, but other than that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be fair to say that there were a lot of people present in camouflage uniform, both male and female; right?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any females, but there may easily have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, can I ask the witness what "the Eagle's Nest" means? Because I think the Chamber has also heard about this Eagle's Nest now for the first time. Where was the Eagle's Nest, exactly, and why was it given that name?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the reason for the name. It was quite high up in the hills, amongst the trees. I don't know if it was simply a nickname or whether what was a former restaurant, I believe, had already had that name. But it was referred to widely in those terms. It was -- I was always taken there on a fairly circuitous route from Vitez. We were led there by police vehicles of various kinds, but it was above Vitez, in the hills, maybe a 15-minute drive by the circuitous route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you were at that headquarters, were there a great number of security people around Mr. Kordic when you, yourself, were there, which would show that he exercised a certain degree of political power?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
