utterances.text: It had all the hallmarks of a headquarters. There were lots of security people around. It was guarded by people in military uniform at the checkpoints on the way up. And it was certainly -- it looked like a military planning centre. There were maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, you've stated that the location of this facility was above Vitez; did you actually mean that it was to the south of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always went there from Vitez. I didn't -- -- I was never shown its location on a map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, turning to Prosecution Exhibit Z759,1, which was a videotape that you were shown, I believe of a British mercenary in Mostar, Mostar was Mr. Boban's bailiwick, if we can use that term; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It was certainly much closer to Grude, where Mr. Boban had his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never learned of any facts that would suggest that Mr. Kordic had any power down in that area of the country, down in Mostar, did you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I notice that in the short footage that you were shown regarding the camp at Kaonik, the inmates appeared to be in what looked like a purpose-built military prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not an expert. It was described to me as being a storehouse, but it certainly looked like those rooms were cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you interviewed were smoking cigarettes. Do you know from whom they received those?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of them was smoking a cigarette on the film. That was given to them by the guards at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You stated that you had some conversations with people at a location called the Bungalow. Who did you speak to? What were their names?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were their ranks?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No idea. But they were outside. I was not allow to go in. I asked to go in, but I wasn't allowed to go in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know who that commander was either, do you?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shown two pieces of a videotape right at the end of your testimony in which Mr. Ganic, I believe, said "We, the Muslims, are the majority in this country, and it's up to us, essentially, to take the lead in smoothing over relations with the Croats." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that footage shot in May of 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present during the attack by Muslim forces on the town of Travnik from June the 8th to June the 12th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, Travnik was under attack at various stages during the war, and I was there when it was being shelled on some occasions, but I don't recollect that particular attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that the town was actually captured by Muslim forces on June the 12th and that there were about 3,500 Croat refugees who had to leave the town as a result?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the attack by ABiH forces on the town of Kakanj at around the same time, from June the 9th to June the 13th?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but I wouldn't deny that such attacks took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you any knowledge about the number of refugees, Croat refugees, that resulted from the attacks on that town, sir?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but there certainly were Croat refugees. I met and interviewed too many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple of final questions to finish up. Were you aware of an attack on the town of Fojnica by Muslim forces in July of 1993 and the capture of that town as a result?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware there was an action by a unit of the Bosnian army, and there was a term used at the time, "Black Swans," for one of the units, but I have no evidence as to what that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you've never heard of the Black Swans as a special purpose unit of the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indication was that that's who they were, but I didn't meet them. I did go up into Fojnica perhaps a little after that. There was a hospital in Fojnica which was surrounded for a time by Croatian forces, and that was one story that we did because some of these people were mentally disabled. I went also into a village near Fojnica to meet one of the units there. So we went there, but I can't give you many valuable details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any dealings with members of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I must have done, but I don't -- because they were certainly one of the Muslim army units, one of the Bosnian army units operating in that region, and they had a reputation after a while for toughness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They also had a reputation for lots of foreign Mujahedin serving in that unit as well, did they not?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think "lots" is an exaggeration. There certainly were those. I already described to you that I encountered them. Of course, the whole situation became radicalised as the war went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the subject of the release of prisoners that you discussed in the middle of May of 1993 in Zenica, isn't it true that members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, approximately 100 of them, were in attendance, firing in the air, and basically acting in a lawless fashion, and that's why you were told to leave the area immediately?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. There was no firing. There may have been. I don't know what happened afterwards, but certainly there were -- I wouldn't say 100. I only saw about 12 fighters dressed unconventionally. The exchange took place in the carpark of the Hotel International in Zenica, which was close to the stadium, and the stadium wall was ringed by, I'd say, a dozen of these unconventionally dressed people who did not look superficially to be from Bosnia. On the ground, there was, as I referred to earlier, this anti-aircraft gun which was operated -- and that seemed to me to be operated by a Bosnian; he looked, as much as one can judge, to be a Bosnian. But it was pointed directly at us, and it seemed a judicious time to leave. I didn't see any firing. I didn't see any firing; I didn't hear any firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the subject of the Croat refugees from the town of Kakanj in June of 1993, were you aware that they had migrated northwards to the town of Vares?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't -- I knew that Vares was, for a time, I don't know about isolated, but it certainly was in Croatian defence force hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That town fell to Muslim forces on November the 2nd of 1993; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that but -- November 1993? I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Damon. My name is Goran Mikulicic, and in these proceedings, alongside Mr. Kovacic, I represent the accused, Mr. Mario Cerkez. Would you please be so kind, Mr. Damon, and tell us whether you ever personally had a conversation with Mr. Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recollect ever having such a conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what position, during your stay in Central Bosnia, Mr. Cerkez occupied?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not beyond he was a senior figure, according to those people to whom I spoke, but, no, I had no dealings with him. His name came up in conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity to see a written document signed by him?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recollect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, you said that during these events, you were a freelance journalist and that you reported for SkyNews and Fox News. What did you do after 1993?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued to report for -- those two that you mentioned were, in fact, linked. They were both part of the Murdoch empire. I also reported for other organisations, and I continue to do that. How long would you like me to go on? Your question said "after 1993." Perhaps you could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically, what do you do today, Mr. Damon?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a reporter and presenter for BBC World service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Damon, during the course of your evidence, a videotape was played. This was an exercise or a parade of the HVO units, which was introduced as Exhibit 257.1. Do you remember this videotape?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where and when this tape was filmed?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "When" is the date on the tape box. I don't think there's any dispute about that. We always dated the tape labels immediately. "Where," I don't know. I wasn't involved in the filming. I sent the crew to cover it with a translator. I was covering another story. So "where," no, I was told it was inside Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific? Was it in Central Bosnia? Was it in the southwestern Bosnia, in Herzegovina, or some other place?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the journey they had to make was quite a way down southwest, but I really can't be more precise. It took them some hours to get there from Vitez where we were based.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the tape was made several hours' drive away from Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On 16 April, 1993, they were the events in Ahmici. We will address that. You told us during your testimony that this event and the fighting in Vitez, for you, according to the information you received from the U.N. representatives, was a surprise of sorts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a "sudden escalation" is the words I used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, do you recall where were you staying in that time; that is, several days before 16 April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to travel from Tuzla in the direction of that area of Vitez, Travnik, Novi Travnik, or Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came as soon as the news of the events of Ahmici reached us, maybe the following day. I travelled down immediately to Ahmici, directly, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the way to Ahmici, did you encounter any problems? Here, I'm referring to the checkpoints or blockades or something like that on the road.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several checkpoints, but no blockading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity in the period between 13 and 16 April, 1993 to travel outside of Zenica in that general direction?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recollect. I think I was in Tuzla also at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even though you did not travel, did you know that the roads from Zenica to Novi Travnik and further on to Vitez had been blocked by the BH army units? Do you know of that fact?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, you said that you visited Ahmici on two occasions. My question to you is this: Do you know the fact that on 16 April, 1993, which was the day of the conflict in Ahmici, there was also fighting in the villages of Poculica, Grbavica, Sivrino Selo, Kruscica, the surrounding villages? Do you know of those locations?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details of those locations. I probably did at the time, but I don't recollect. I couldn't point them out on a map at this stage. I didn't know that -- I knew that there was a conflagration along the valley. I had been informed of that by my BBC colleague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in this area, Mr. Damon, did you meet Major Andrew Williams, who was with BritBat?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the events on your second visit in Ahmici, when you said that you were surprised by the clearing of the terrain which was in progress on the ground. Do you know that this clearing of the terrain had been arranged for with BritBat several days earlier?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that was my third visit, and I didn't know of any arrangements. There certainly were, to my observation, no international personnel there at the time, and I suppose my suspicion was aroused because we were stopped from filming it. What you say may, indeed, be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, you mentioned -- in your testimony you said that some perpetrators from Ahmici were known to the U.N. investigators. How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told by the U.N. investigators that they had names on the day that I went to Ahmici with Colonel Bob Stewart and the European Union, European Community ambassadors. I was subsequently given those names some months later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that you received a list of individuals suspected of having committed the crimes in Ahmici from the U.N. investigators?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't get it from the U.N. investigators. I did receive a list of four names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have this list on you today, Mr. Damon?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with me at the moment, but I could get hold of it, if it's not known to the Court. I'm sure that it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that you would be willing, if asked by the Tribunal, to produce this list?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would, certainly. I think, as I say, I would just like to repeat, I believe the Tribunal must have this list because the source from which I got it is known to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything to prevent you from telling us who gave you that list?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, at this stage, in open court, I wouldn't want to do that. But in principle, no, there's nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would suggest that we go into private session so that the witness can answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, you've said that during your stay in Ahmici, you saw a box of military equipment with an inscription on it. Do you read Chinese?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred to the Chinese, I believe, in relation to Busovaca, when I was in the hills above Busovaca, at some later time. I didn't refer to it in relation to Ahmici. And no, I don't read Chinese.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, I misunderstood you. Mr. Damon, you spoke to us about the prisoner exchange that you attended in Zenica. Zenica was a town under the absolute control of the BH army; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that in that exchange, in an important capacity, a military unit was present which obviously was a unit that did not belong to the BH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to whom they belonged. They were not wearing conventional Bosnian army uniform. And as I mentioned to you, I went subsequently to the police chief in Zenica and asked him why these people appeared to be operating with such aggression in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also present were members of the British Battalion, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any representative of the BH army present?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, obviously, during your stay in Bosnia in those days, you travelled extensively; would it be true to say that? Is it also true that on many occasions you made the trip from Bosnia to the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's true, in both cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us which routes you took in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two main routes: one through Jablanica, which I believe in that time to which we are referring was harder, and one through Gornji Vakuf, and then, on a long dirt road, down to Tomislavgrad. Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, and Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from there on to Split, I assume?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Damon, if, for instance, you were to set off from Split to go to Vitez, you would cover a long road. Along that road, did you come across checkpoints held by HVO soldiers and by members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct in both cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Damon, did you ever -- and I'm not referring to your visit to Bosnia when you came to Pale by helicopter, but the period covered by the end of '92 and the whole of '93 -- did you go to the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you enter that territory from any other side except from the side of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally we would fly into Sarajevo by aid flight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, maybe my question was confusing. I was thinking of land routes, not air routes.

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe in that period there were other ways except through Split. There may have been, but we didn't try. Split was a useful logistical base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to infer that those same routes that you used were used by convoys of humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Damon, that all those convoys of aid which were not delivered by air came from the territory of the Republic of Croatia to the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was for a time a route from Banja Luka across Serb lines at Turbe. I didn't travel it; it was only available for UNHCR vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, Mr. Damon, you spent quite some time in Bosnia. You witnessed that civil war, and in answer to Mr. Sayers' question whether it was confusing, you said, "not really." Could you tell us, in very general terms -- and I have in mind the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole -- who among the ethnic groups there was fighting whom?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There -- at certain stages, all the different -- well, all three communities, who identified themselves as Serbian, Muslim, or Croatian, were variously engaged in fighting. But there was a sequence, as you know, and the sequence is important. I don't believe I should take the time of the Court; they are aware of the sequence. But it's important to recognise there was a sequence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite clear, Mr. Damon. Is it true that in one period of time, the Muslims and Croats were fighting the Serbs together?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true that in another period of time, the Serbs were fought separately by the Muslims and the Croats, each one of them separately?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosnia as a whole, I'm sure that was the case, yes, there were areas where HVO was fighting Serbs alone and also where the Bosnian army was fighting Serbs alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, are you familiar with the northwestern part of Bosnia, called the Cazin Krajina, with the leading figure there being Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in relation to that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslims fought amongst themselves, one group against another, which means within the same ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- what I know is that one particular ambitious leader was encouraged, and I saw this encouragement for myself, by both Serbs and by Croats to try to establish his own enclave in order to weaken the Bosnian government in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that politician was a Muslim by ethnicity, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- he was a Muslim by ethnicity and a capitalist by inclination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that confusing, after all, Mr. Damon?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where are we going with this, Mr. Mikulicic?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all confusing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply wanted to demonstrate to this Chamber that the situation in Bosnia is anything but simple, and with that, I would end my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we got the witness's answer. Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, about three questions. Re-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, following up on a question by Mr. Sayers, can you say what Mr. Kordic's other fears were, if you remember that part of the questioning?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean, other than what I've already stated, that there was a fear -- the Defence counsel referred to the proportion of the Croatian population in the region and also the increase in the Muslim population as a result of refugees arriving in the area from eastern Bosnia. So this was the given justification for the fears.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question. What was your observation about Mr. Kordic's personality?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's based on the few meetings that I had. He was, quite clearly, highly motivated, intelligent, he was cold and calculating in his answers to my questions about what was going on, and I should say, above all, he was clearly in charge. He had an air of authority about him, and people around him deferred to him. If he asked for something to be done, it was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Kaonik on the 14th of May, 1993, did anyone challenge or question Mr. Kordic's authority to give you permission to be there?

utterances.speaker: DANIEL DAMON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Damon, thank you for coming to the Tribunal again and giving your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just put one issue on the agenda? We were trying -- I mean, the Defence and the Prosecutor -- to find a solution for the timing of the testimony of the next witness after the one who is just prepared, (redacted). It seems that it easily may be that we will be very much squeezed for time, because if that witness will start, and realistically it will, let's say tomorrow at lunchtime, shortly after the break or before the break, then we will be left, the Defence will be left with very, very limited time for cross-examination, and the Prosecution told us that the witness (redacted) said that he would be coming either now or never and that he has to leave The Hague before the weekend. Your Honour, this witness is probably among the ten most important witnesses for our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was a commander of some sort; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, he was a politician in Vitez. We surely will need a little bit more for cross than perhaps an hour or two on Friday morning. I'm not mentioning also the problem that Cerkez won't be here, because we will prepare, and it's not crucial. The crucial point is only to have a decent amount of time, a reasonable time, and I leave it up to you after you hear the testimony. But I'm trying to anticipate the problem, and I know that we will be squeezed because at a certain point in time, the Prosecution, confirmed by the witness, will tell us, everyone in the courtroom, "Well, he has to be back during the weekend and he cannot return."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate you would require in cross-examination with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could give you only really a rough estimation, but I guess a couple of hours, I'm sure. He is talking about the whole period of the development of events in Vitez, and the most important time, April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you assist, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm aware of the difficulties. There are a number of difficulties with witnesses this week, including other difficulties with the witness who might come between the one that Mr. Lopez-Terres is just about to call and the witness that's been referred to here. On top of those difficulties, there's the reality that once people are here, their hard attitudes sometimes soften. We will make every arrangement between now and first thing tomorrow morning to ensure that the problems with the witness that Mr. Kovacic has been speaking of are properly addressed, and I'll report back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be, without being any more elliptical than is necessary, it may be that the intervening witness, the one who will come after this witness, will, for other reasons, which are referred to obliquely in the application for protective measures in his case, will not be fit to give evidence this week, but might be fit perhaps next week. That depends on medical issues being resolved. It is always difficult juggling the range of problems with witnesses and ensuring that the Chamber's time is fully occupied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, the witness that Mr. Kovacic has just spoken about, is he in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but he'll be here tonight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: He will be here tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, couldn't you give him priority, because apparently he can't remain longer than this week, tomorrow morning so that Mr. Kovacic could make the necessary and proper preparations, either tomorrow afternoon or on Friday morning? We have tomorrow and then Friday morning, so it's up to you to organise things so that that witness is given priority, if he, in fact, is here tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind, and I have to juggle the various problems with the various witnesses. Perhaps Mr. Lopez-Terres can deal with the application for protective measures for the next witness, but I think that although he's only seeking qualified protection, a fully closed session for the application might be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake. I think private session will do because, of course, we don't need the screens down. Nothing is going to be shown. If it's a private session, I think that saves time. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres, I think you can begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I wanted to ask the usher if he can give the document to the witness so that we can be sure that he is who he is supposed to be. Examined by Mr. Lopez-Terres:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the name on this document, in fact, your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You are appearing here with the pseudonym "Witness K"; therefore, I'm going to call you Witness K?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, are you 60 years old?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you work, starting in 1976, as a technician within the SPS factory in Vitez, and are you currently retired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but the year is not correct. It was 1976 and I did not work for the steel mill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I had said 1976. Perhaps there was an interpretation problem. It doesn't matter. It isn't important. Witness K, you live in Ahmici, you've always lived in that village, and you knew most of the people who lived there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After April 1993, did you make an important contribution to the establishment of an association of former inhabitants of Ahmici, where you are still living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, is it correct that you were a member of the Communist Party until 1968?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, you decided to leave that party. In the 1990s, at the time, there was a plurality of parties allowed in -- introduced into the former Yugoslavia. You became a member of the SDA party, that is, the Bosnian Muslim party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you still a member of that party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, the village of Ahmici is about five kilometres from Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1993, was the population of that village approximately 600 people, most of whom were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 40 Bosnian Croats living in that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Ahmici, is it divided in two parties, Upper Ahmici and Lower Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct, and that is the division that actually is a new one. Previously it wasn't so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upper Ahmici was the older part of it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1993 there were two mosques in the village in Ahmici. One had a minaret and the other one did not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The one with the minaret was the one that was in Lower Ahmici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around the end of 1992, Witness K, did you, yourself, and other Muslims working at the SPS factory in Vitez, were you able to see that the Croats in the factory were gradually taking responsibilities in that place, and specifically that they had set up a flag, little by little, in that factory? Could you remind us of how things or tell us about how things happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Immediately after the multinational elections of 1990, one started feeling --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm simply asking you to tell us what happened in the factory, about the flag that was put up in the facilities of the factory.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, the whole atmosphere at that time already was smacking of divisions. Many employees, especially those who had to do with security, were being transferred, so that they did not have anything to do with security. They had a wish to put up a Croatian flag. This irritated the Muslim employees. They did this gradually. When entering the factory, I first saw it in a drawer. Then, for several days, then it was on a chair, and then it ended up on the desk of the department head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that same time, approximately, was it a unit that was composed only of Croat workers who were responsible for guarding the factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: These were not factory employees. These were the so-called special security personnel. They were not locals. They were brought in from outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the Muslim workers who formerly had been responsible for guarding the factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I have already stated that they were transferred -- in other words, they were offered to be transferred to other sections within the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like us to speak about the things that happened on the 19th of October, 1992. On that afternoon, while you were coming back from your job at the factory, you were arrested at a checkpoint which had been set up at the place known as Impregnacija, and you noticed that at that checkpoint, the HVO soldiers had set up heavy weapons. There was a cannon, there was a machine gun, there was also an anti-aircraft gun that was in front of the police station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That evening, coming back from work, I was driving a car. In addition to Impregnacija, I had cleared another checkpoint, but down there, and I cleared it. I was then stopped along with everybody else. They were searching all the cars. However, I was fortunate to have found a colleague from the factory who did not check me at all. He just told me, "Okay, go on." It is true that there were some heavy weapons there. There was an antitank gun which was -- an anti-aircraft gun on a vehicle, mounted on a vehicle. This vehicle patrolled the entire territory of the municipality, wherever they could take it, but I mostly saw it in front of the police station, parked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were able to go past the checkpoint and go home to Ahmici, and there you were invited to participate in a meeting with other villagers from the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the meeting organised at the request of the person responsible for the Territorial Defence of the village, Mr. Fuad Berbic, who then told you, and told other people as well, that an oral order had been given by the Bosnian army in command in Vitez in order to set up a checkpoint in order to prevent reinforcements from the HVO coming from Busovaca and Kiseljak being able to go in the direction of Novi Travnik? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct. May I just add a brief comment? This barricade was probably ordered to be erected, but taking into account all the circumstances, and considering that we were in grave danger, and that our village was touching on the main road, and that we were wedged in or sandwiched between two much more largely populated Croat villages, the whole situation smacked of something bad, and we decided not to put up the barricade. So this barricade, even though an order had been issued to erect it, it was not erected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the checkpoint was not initially set up, but subsequently, during the evening, it finally was set up by people, after two reserve policemen from Ahmici came and told the other villagers that they had been disarmed by the HVO, and this made the people change their decision as to the setting up of the checkpoint; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, it is so, but those men who were there -- for a while it was jointly manned, the barricade between the Muslims and the Croats, and at some point towards the evening, the two men who were from our village were disarmed, they were abused, and they were kicked out, so to speak, and sent home. When they came back, they were so frustrated and so angry that without any approval, with probably some of those who agreed with them, they set up a barricade. I think that the intention was to get in possession of some weapons, and I think that they didn't know of Fuad's order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the end, the barricade or the checkpoint was set up by two policemen and a group of young men from the village. And as regards the weapons that the people had, basically there were a few machine guns, and you also said that those people had also put some metal pipes on the road so that the HVO would make a mistake and think that they were dealing with mortars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that same evening, is it true that the men who were first there, that's the men from Ahmici, were joined by about 30 other people from neighbouring villages -- 10 who came from Vrhovine, 10 who came from Poculica, and 10 from the village of Preocica -- and that those men took up positions at different locations in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct. And again I would like to add a brief comment to this. Probably the command which had ordered this had believed that since we were unarmed, they probably thought that we needed some assistance, so they had assigned these men from these villages to come and join in the effort. However, we went out to meet them, to tell them not to come, because we didn't need them; but they had taken a different route in, and so indeed they were there that night with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, not participate in that, Mr. K?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the next day, 20 October, 1992, around 5.00, the fighting began, and the first shell fell onto the minaret of the Lower Ahmici mosque; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct, because later on we heard that the HVO were under orders -- they had a plan called "24 Hours of Ashes and Smoke," and this was to start when the morning call to prayer was to start. And when imam called the believers to the mosque was exactly the time when the first shell was fired on the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you, yourself, were in the village, were you able to see that there were guns being fired at Ahmici, guns that were firing from the neighbouring villages of Hrasno and Donji Rovna, which are in the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also see that truck on which there was a gun, a gun had been mounted, that you spoke about a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was firing coming from that truck with the gun on top of it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had already seen that truck, with the gun which had been mounted on it, on several occasions in the village of Ahmici, and the truck would come now and again, apparently in order to make an impression on the local population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They often appeared in the village with this vehicle. And the driver, who was given to drinking -- his name was Nikica Plavcic; we used to call him Nikica Slikica -- and probably slightly inebriated, he circled around with that gun there and went through the village, trying to impress us, to actually produce fear among us from this great power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the morning of 20 October, 1992, at around 10.00 in the morning, the local HVO commander, whose name was Buha and lived in Buhine Kuce, gave an ultimatum to the TO soldiers, telling them to surrender the weapons that they had; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct. There were agreements -- there was a meeting to try to determine what to do next, and then Fuad Berbic and the others who were, how shall I put it, in charge of our village, they had talked, and the HVO commander ordered that we Bosniaks had to surrender the weapons that we did have and that they would guarantee our security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of the Muslim villagers who lived in the area called Zume agreed to surrender their weapons, but in Ahmici, the inhabitants who had some weapons refused to do so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That's correct. Those who had surrendered, they were from the part of the village which was mixed, Croat and Muslim, and the ones up there were more compactly inhabited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They refused to give their arms and the fighting continued, and during the battle, there were about 14 buildings and stables which were destroyed by fire, because inflammable ammunition was being used, and shells also fell into five or six houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The houses were set on fire. They didn't burn down to the ground, but certain rooms were burned, as most of those incendiary devices flew in through the windows. Sometimes some barns, even there was some livestock which was burnt. So there were several of those cases when people didn't have the time to let the livestock out. Clearly and obviously, the people pulled back into the upper part of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself withdraw with some of the other villagers to the upper part of the village, and from that part of Upper Ahmici, were you able to try to ask for help by radio, ask the Vitez centre, but that no assistance was sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you finally able to leave the village of Ahmici and go to the village of Vrhovine, a neighbouring village, where you remained for about five or six days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: About 90 per cent of the inhabitants went up to that part of the village. Some did stay behind, and fortunately, nothing happened to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the fighting on the 19th, 20th of October, 1992, one of your cousins, a 16-year-old, (redacted), was killed by a bullet, and two other people were wounded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct. Can I just add something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: (redacted) was in high school; he was a young kid. As a man, though, I don't know, he probably was under the influence of some movies or something, so he had some fighting spirit in him. So he wanted to see what was going on at the barricade, and as a civilian, he went over there to see and survey what was going on, and somebody killed him with sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean that your cousin was not armed at the point he was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. He was a youth; he was still in the secondary school. He didn't have any weapons or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the only victim on the Muslim side that day? There were two wounded, I think, and then this cousin who died.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Two were wounded and this young man was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the villagers of Ahmici were in the neighbouring village for the few days that you spent in Vrhovine, was it the HVO military police that entered the village and took measures to ensure that there would be no thefts in the houses, and you were able to see when you came back that nothing had been stolen from your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That's correct. They protected our houses, and, indeed, nothing went missing from our homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're moving on now to another topic, it may be a convenient moment. We will adjourn now until half past two. Witness K, could you remember, in this and any other adjournment there is, not to speak to anybody about your evidence and not to let anybody speak to you about it, and that includes members of the Prosecution? Very well. If you will be back at half past two. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m. 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, before we broke, we were speaking about the end of the events in October 1992 and the first incident in the village after the checkpoint which had been set up in Ahmici. When you returned to the village, you noticed that Croatian flags had been set up there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before that, the flags were not there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. Excuse me. It is correct that there were no such flags. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other flags in the village, before the events of the 19th of October, 1992, that is, specifically, the flag of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: There were on the school and other such buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A public building then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometime after the attack of October 1992, you had the opportunity of meeting with one of your neighbours, a man named Vlatko Kupreskic, who is currently being detained in The Hague and is the subject of a trial which we spoke about this morning, and you asked him for some information about what had happened, why that had happened. Is it true that at that point, he said to you that in the future, the Muslims had to obey the law of Herceg-Bosna because Herceg-Bosna was now a state, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had become a state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Exactly. I wasn't alone. I was in a group; there were another four of us, among them my father. Because he was closest to our village, as our neighbour, we asked him what was happening because there was already the ultimatum that we had to surrender our weapons, practically to surrender ourselves, and his answer was that the state of Herceg-Bosna had been established. "You have to respect its laws," he said. "How long it will last, I don't know, but why things are as they are, you have to be loyal to that state." That is what he said, or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that period between November 1992 and January 1993, there was an agreement among the inhabitants of Ahmici, according to which there would be checkpoints that would be manned both by the Croats and the Muslims from the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Correct. These were not stationary checkpoints but rather patrols that patrolled the villages in the evenings, and we were together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Witness K, that around November 1992, you saw the accused, Dario Kordic, during a press conference in which he was a participant which was broadcast on Busovaca Television and in which there was also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two objections, Your Honour. First, to the leading form of the question, since this is a matter that appears to be in controversy, and, second, I object to having a phrase snipped out of what appears to be a televised press conference. Of course, we would not object to having the videotape and the transcript of the entire press conference put into evidence, but I certainly object on completeness grounds to having one statement that was assertively made six years ago in a press conference excerpted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness be asked if he saw Dario Kordic on the press conference and, if so, what he recollects Mr. Kordic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I speak to the witness, if you will allow me, Mr. President, I can tell you that the Office of the Prosecutor does not have a videocassette of that press conference. I want things to be perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, during the press conference in which you were a participant, do you remember what the accused, Dario Kordic, from the point that they were speaking about the village of Ahmici, said, what he said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't know the date when this was. I never thought I would be put in a situation as to have to testify about these things. But I do remember, since my village did receive Busovaca Television -- not too well, but still we were able to follow it -- we were curious to see what they were saying and what they had in mind for us, and at one of those press conferences, Dario Kordic was present, as was Kostroman and Blaskic, and there were a number of journalists. Among the other questions, there was a question to the effect -- of course, I can't quote it verbatim because of the time distance -- but the question was, "After the barricade in Ahmici, what would happen to the village of Ahmici?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the objection now, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's my point precisely, Your Honour. That actually brings me into a Rule 89 objection. If the gentleman can't remember exactly what the statement was on the TV, it seems to me that the prejudicial effect of the statement that apparently he's going to utter, according to this offer of proof, greatly outweighs any probative value that it might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why? It's as if he met Mr. Kordic and Mr. Kordic said something to him. He saw him say something on television. He cannot remember the precise words, but he can give us the gist of it. There's no unfairness in that. Now, what do you remember Mr. Kordic saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Of course, I wasn't with him physically. I was in my own home and watching television. In answer to this question which was put, I think, by a lady journalist, he answered that Ahmici would pay a dear price for this move; that is, for the barricade they had put up. As I said, I can't quote him word for word, but to the effect that it would be razed to the ground, that they'd better be careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, I believe we have perhaps an interpretation problem here. You yourself were not at the press conference. You were at home; is that correct? Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because in the English transcript, one has the impression that you were present, at least at the moment that the press conference occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the picture is quite clear. The witness was not participating, although that appeared to be what was said. He was simply at home and saw this on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Still speaking about the television broadcast that you were looking at at that time, did you also see a broadcast around January or February of 1993, during which a man named Anto Valenta was invited -- it was a programme in Croatia from Split -- and Anto Valenta, during that programme, said that the Croats in Bosnia should, in the future, make ready for the conflict with the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It was a programme called "Image on Image," and the guest was Anto Valenta. But I must make a correction. He didn't say the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina; he said the Croats of Vitez must prepare for a struggle against the Muslims. He made this statement upon his return because some people asked him whether he had made a slip of the tongue, whether he really meant that they should prepare for defence against a Serb aggression, but he said what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see, somewhat later in the spring of 1993, the accused, Dario Kordic, during another press conference, also mentioning the relations between the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia? Could you tell us what was said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: At that time, he was a prominent media figure, he appeared frequently, and we watched from time to time, and at another press conference, a journalist -- I think that was the time when we were trying to obtain seeds for the sowing season -- and the journalist was saying, "The Muslims are sowing everywhere and we are short of seeds," something to that effect, and his answer was, "Let them sow and we shall harvest," that the Croats would reap the harvest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he said "they can sow," he meant the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, 1993, Mr. K, your son, who at that time was working at the Bratsvo factory in Novi Travnik, was arrested by HVO soldiers, along with a group of other factory workers while they were going to the factory in a bus; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Correct. He was going to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the next day, the day after his arrest, your son and the group of Muslim workers visited Mario Cerkez in his office at the cinema in Vitez, at the House of Culture?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Maybe the interpretation is not correct. It wasn't he that went to visit. I went to pay the visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it was an interpretation difficulty. Did you go to visit the accused, Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: The interpretation I got was that he went to visit, and he couldn't visit because he had already been arrested. So it was I who went to visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You, not your son, did you go to visit Mario Cerkez? Do we agree on that, that it was you who went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you visited Mario Cerkez, whom you knew, and you asked him whether he could release or help in the release of your son. Could you speak about that meeting of 14 April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I could. My son, as is known, was working in Bratsvo, and on the way to work, they were stopped by a group of HVO soldiers, of the police, at a checkpoint. They ordered all the Muslims to get off the bus, the Croats were allowed to pass, and they were detained. At that time, I was in my own factory. One of his colleagues who went to school with him and who was also a Catholic, a Croat, informed me that they had been arrested, that he had been arrested or captured. I immediately left my working place and went to some sort of TO headquarters to see Sefkija Dzidic. I appealed to him as a parent to help me to get my son released because he was not guilty. As he couldn't make any promises, I went to see Pero Skopljak, who, in those days, was the president of the HDZ, or something like that, and literally, his answer was, "I am a politician and I can't help you. This is a military matter." I used to work with Mario in the factory. We are not the same generation, so we were not very close, but we know one another very well. I also know his parents. So I went to the place where his headquarters was, and with a soldier, I went to see him. The man received me in a friendly manner and he said the following: "Regarding so and so, not a hair will be hurt on his head. Last night, a number of our officers were arrested in Gornji Vakuf, and they were taken for the purpose of exchange. I cannot help you for the moment, but you can count on him being safe and sound," and that was the whole conversation, so I left. My son, on the 15th in the evening, together with another 50 Bosniaks, was taken to the camp in Kaonik, which belongs to Busovaca municipality, and he was kept there for two months. He was mistreated, of course. He was forced to dig trenches, et cetera; he was slapped, beaten, and all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your son remained in the Kaonik camp for about two months, and you say that he dug trenches specifically in the region of Kratina and Putis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, in Putis, yes. Once he even went to the area of Rovna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, 1993, Witness K, around 5.30 in the morning, in the village where you lived, you heard a large explosion and there were bullets flying from all sides. You could see at that point that there were several houses around yours that were on fire. You did not expect an attack on that day, on the 16th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is so. The night before, we had a meeting, we the locals without any politicians, in our school, us ordinary citizens, and we agreed to protect each other, that any kind of attack was out of the question, so that we went to bed without the thought of such a thing happening -- occurring to us. My son was in the camp without being registered, and there were already cases of people being killed, so it was terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, during the night of 15 to 16 April, 1993 that we're speaking about, Muslim forces arrived in Ahmici; they were deployed in Ahmici or around Ahmici. Now, I'm talking about Muslim army forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. No, there were absolutely no troops in our village. Our village was, in no sense, a military target. There were only civilians there, and the few able-bodied men that we had in the village, since a Muslim army brigade had already been formed, they had left and joined that unit. So even they were not in the village. The only people in the village were my generation, in their 50s and 60s and older than that, and women and children, and the few who were not able-bodied to join the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, we have just spoken about the night of the 15th to 16th of April, 1993. Let us speak about the previous night, that is, the 14th to the 15th of April. I'll ask the same question: Did forces from the Bosnia-Herzegovina army -- rather, were the forces deployed in Ahmici or around Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, a hundred times, no. I said that there were no soldiers there, and I say that categorically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document. This is Z6601. The document is a preparatory combat order, and it's dated 15, April 1993, 10.00, and it's signed by Colonel Blaskic. Witness K, would you review the first page of the document, the fourth paragraph of the document? There, the date of 14/15 April 1993 is indicated, where they speak about deployment of Muslim forces in the region of Ahmici and Nadioci. The document says that the troops of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina allegedly were deployed around the village, and that you are sure, however, that there was no deployment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: This is a complete fallacy. In our village and the environs, there was not a single armed soldier under the control of the BH army or the TO. And I am reading this now, it mentions the village of Nadioci. Ninety-eight per cent of that village were Croats. It was 98 per cent Croat, and what would any Muslim army be doing there? I can tell you for certain that in our village, there were absolutely no military structures, or around the village. In Stari Vitez, possibly there were, and in Kruscica, a part of a brigade had been formed, but that is quite at the other end of the area. In Kruscica, there were troops because my brother's son was there in a unit in Kruscica. As for Vitez, I don't know. I assume there may have been some, but in Nadioci and Ahmici, there were absolutely none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, were troops from outside of Vitez, from Zenica or other regions, did they come in and might they have been deployed in Ahmici or the surroundings in the night between the 14th and 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, they could not because members of the HVO had already, at Kuber, which is a hill between Vitez and Zenica, they already had their positions there, so that their army had control of that part of the territory, the whole area around Ahmici. So there was no way that anybody from the outside could reach us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us return to the evening of the 15th of April, 1993, the evening. During the evening, you saw Croatian neighbours who were armed, who had weapons, had combat uniforms, were wearing helmets, and they were going to the part of the village where the Kupreskic family lived, but did that not seem somewhat suspect to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That evening, my brother and I went out to walk around the houses. In the evening, it was already dusk, visibility was good, and I saw my next-door neighbour, Dragan Vidovic, and his cousin in full combat gear, with weapons, a rucksack, a helmet on the rucksack, going in haste towards the Kupreskic houses, as we call it. But we didn't attach much importance to that because they would frequently -- or, rather, the HVO army could frequently be seen in the area of our village, and weekly or at other intervals, they would pass through to the positions at Kuber. They passed through our village and nobody hindered them, and then they would return from those positions along the same route. And so we thought that that was what was happening then too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the morning of the 16th of April, the morning of the attack, with your wife and another group of villagers, you decided to take shelter in the house of another villager, Mr. Kermo, who lived in Upper Ahmici, close to the mosque; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct. This house was designated by our civilian protection to be used in case of such an event, and this is where we would go and this is what we used this morning and went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your wife and group of villagers, did you then go along a ditch and through the bushes, but did you see that your presence had been spotted by HVO soldiers near Vlatko Kupreskic's house, and one of the soldiers yelled something at you. Could you tell us what it was that he said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: We were 14 in this group, my family and two other families, so we had no idea that these soldiers could be there. We were going down a ravine, and when we came to this house, they noticed us. They cursed our balija mothers. They were asking where had we been hiding until then, and then opened up fire in bursts on us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was at that time of those shots that were directed against you that your sister-in-law was killed and that your daughter was wounded, along with another person who was a refugee from Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you finally reached the house where you were supposed to take shelter, where there were about 150 to 200 people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct. I took the little girl -- put her on my back and took her with me, and we joined the other people. There were about 150 people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the morning, around 12.00 noon, UNPROFOR came into the village, and the personnel from that vehicle came to the village and helped some of the villagers there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Several vehicles arrived, and one of them turned off towards Kermo's building, because we were waving, asking them to come and help us, and so they came over and assisted the three wounded persons. Then they put them on the transport vehicle and took them to the hospital. And one personnel vehicle proceeded to the other part of the village on the other side of the hill, where there were also two seriously wounded persons. One died there and the other one died while being transported to Travnik. Both were females.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice that the shots from the HVO had stopped throughout the time that that transport vehicle was there, and then once the vehicle had left, the shots resumed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: This was especially the case of the heavy artillery in Hrasno and Donja Rovna. They almost completely ceased to fire, and you could just hear some small arms fire. But the heavy artillery practically ceased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around 21.00 on that day, with a group of villagers, you left Kermo's house, and then in groups of about ten persons, you were able to flee and to reach the village of Vrhovine, and then to go to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct. Because we expected, frankly, some kind of assistance from Zenica or Vitez, and since this assistance was not coming and we had hundreds of dead, there was panic in the village, houses were on fire, there was fire everywhere, we decided to flee in groups. Night was coming, so those who were healthier and stronger were sent up to the village to see whether we had been cut off by the HVO forces in order to prevent our pull-out. They came back; they said that the road was open and we went in groups to the village of Vrhovine. However, some families, including my parents, stayed behind, and unfortunately, they're no longer among us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, as I already said, you already had the occasion of testifying in another case; that is, the Kupreskic case last year in September, and on that occasion, you made an important contribution to the drafting of documents, which I'm now going to show to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They have already been tendered to the Trial Chamber which is hearing the Kupreskic case. These are charts with reference number Z1594, 1-5-9-4, 1594-3. And the two aerial views of the village of Ahmici and the surroundings on which there is information about the houses which the Muslims in the village occupied, and the houses in which people were killed or they were the owners of houses who were killed at that time. This is reference 1594-1 and 1594-2. . I ask that these documents be put under seal because all of them have the witness's name on them, as well as his signature which is on one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to tell us what this document corresponds to. First of all, we're going to look at the two aerial views I've mentioned. Witness K, the two aerial views which you have, the two views --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- as I said, you helped to prepare them because it was starting with information that you provided that the Office of the Prosecutor was in a position to prepare those two aerial views and to show the indications on them, that is, exactly where the houses belonging to the Muslims in Ahmici were, that's on the first map. And on the second, it shows where people were killed in Ahmici. Do you recognise these two documents as being the ones that you helped to prepare and that you brought to the attention of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on what you said, the houses which are in a green circle, they belonged to the Muslim inhabitants of the village you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct. Those were the Muslim homes. Shall I point them out?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary unless the Trial Chamber wishes. As things stand, we don't have to make any further clarifications about the houses. As regards the red circles, these are houses or at least the areas in which there were Croat houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically, the houses of the accused in the Kupreskic case; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second aerial view which is similar, but which has indications in yellow --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the houses where there were victims on the -- on that evening, the 16th of April, and there were Roman numerals to indicate the people who died; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, you also helped to prepare another chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, can I ask, in relation to the first aerial view, F and G, the red circles which are bigger circles, does the size of the circle indicate a greater congregation of houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The areas correspond to the location where the witness believes that the houses of someone named Nenad Santic, who has since died, who was a Croat of the village, from a point where he was exactly not sure where the house was, that he would simply indicate the area, and it's starting with that information that those areas were able to be indicated by our investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards the chart number Z1594-3, is that, in fact, your signature which is on the first page, on the bottom, Witness K?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which is before the date 21 September, 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this document, on the last page, a total is given, that is, 104 people whose names appear in the document, 104 people who were killed in the village, according to the information that you were able to provide.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct and that is really the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the 104 people, tell me if I'm wrong, there were 61 men, 32 women --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and 11 boys under the age of 18?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Ages three months to less than eighteen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also indicated the number of people who were wounded who are not included in the total that I just mentioned, but in that list, there are 12 people who were wounded on the 16th of April, 1993 in Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, during the flight and the withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Personally, Witness K, how many people did you yourself lose in your family during the attack on the village of Ahmici on the 16th of April?
