utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like to add something, that is, if the Chamber approves, before I say this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: We mentioned here a number of 104 killed; however, we know for sure that there were 15 Bosniak refugees who were also killed, and those names are known, but the number of killed refugees was never positively confirmed because these people kept coming and going. So they were not fully registered. So to the number of 104, an additional 15 refugees should be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to make it clear, to make clear this important comment that you've just made, that the number of 104 represents only the 104 members of the village who you knew --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, residents of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the approximately 15 others, the refugees that you spoke about, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: They came from Foca, Prijedor, Karule near Travnik, other places, Jajce, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they? Exactly where were they at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: For the most part, they were accommodated with local residents, and in our area, there were a lot of weekend homes. So we made arrangements with owners of these homes who, for the most part, lived in Zenica, to allow us, meaning this board which had been set up, and they for the most part agreed to this, so these refugees stayed, for the most part, in these weekend areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you a question before you made this important comment. How many people from your own family did you lose during that attack on the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: This is the most difficult part that I can testify to, but I have to, and I lost 19 relatives, including both parents, my mother and father, my brother, his wife, and the others were first cousins on both paternal and maternal side, and they were both male and female relatives among them. I need to mention that my father was 81 years of age. As a man who took good care of his home, he refused to leave. He said, "I had nothing with anybody. They won't do anything to me," and my brother and my mother stayed with him. On the -- that is, around the 20th of April, UNPROFOR brought them to Zenica in body bags, charred, and we made an identification there. I still have some doubts about their identities, but I think I'll leave it alone here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question. The information which allowed this chart to be prepared concerning the location and numbers of people, is this information that you collected as soon as you arrived in Zenica in April 1993 and which you preserved and compiled and then subsequently allowed them to be given to the Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That is correct. I was born in that village; I lived in that village; I know every person there. We worked jointly to bring in the phone lines, water system, roads. We did all this work together, these utilities, so we depended upon each other in the village and knew each other well. Also, when we came to Zenica, we somehow had to take count of who had survived, who was killed, who went to -- in which direction. Until that time, nobody had left to live abroad. I then started an initiative to set up an association which would, sort of, draw people together so that we would stay in touch, so that we could talk about our troubles, and I set up -- I drafted a questionnaire, including the name, date of birth, and the status, that is, their whereabouts. From this questionnaire, we were able to also come up with a number of those who were killed and also it helped us get some humanitarian assistance, which was proportionate to the number of family members; that is, that it became useful in that sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness K.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, the Defence of Mario Cerkez would like to ask questions of this witness first on the basis of an agreement we have with the other part of the defence team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Mikulicic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, I am Goran Mikulicic in this case, alongside Mr. Kovacic from Rijeka, and I represent Mr. Mario Cerkez. First of all, I would like to express my condolences for everything that happened to you and your family.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, are you a religious man? Do you practice your religion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Insofar as I can get around to it, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you are of Islamic faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, at the relevant time, you said that you were a member of the SDA. Are you still a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you have any position within the party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I was only a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, you said that you managed to return to your village. Is it true that your return is part of an organised return of the inhabitants to their village, under a plan set up by Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Let me tell you, if we had waited for our government to start this, we may still not be back. But as citizens who were part of this association, we insisted on going back. And let me tell you, I will also say openly that we had -- there were no obstacles on the part of the local inhabitants -- I don't know what the situation is with the politicians -- but it was in a self-organised way that we really came back, and our government then sort of appropriated it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the question -- what I wanted to point out is that about 70 families returned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I think it's about 90 now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, you said that you worked in the SPS and that it was from there that you knew Mario Cerkez. Do you recall what Mario Cerkez's job at the SPS was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't know whether I'll be able to tell you expertly what exactly his job description was, but I know that it had something to do with defence. It had something to do with the military defence or security for the factory. It had to do with the lists of military conscripts and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that he worked on lists of militarily-fit persons. Does that mean that he worked on administrative work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Among other things, I believe he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, do you know that Mr. Cerkez, at the time when you worked together in the SPS, associated with Midhat Berbic, the son of Fuad Berbic, your close friend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, they were colleagues at work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he also associated with Latif Barucija and Sulejman Kalco?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As well as Sefkija Dzidic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that all the persons whom I have just mentioned are of Muslim ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, let me point out --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Let me point out. This was an entirely normal thing at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is precisely the nature of my question. Did you ever notice whether Mario Cerkez had any kind of bad relations with Muslims, or an attitude towards them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: He is -- he is younger than I am. They associated because they were together at work. They worked in similar jobs. I did not socialise with Mario Cerkez very much, and so far as I did, I had respect for him, and I don't think he's going to be offended if I say that we are friends, and I never noticed any such behaviour on his part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, you mentioned the events when, in the night between the 19th and 20th of October, 1992, a barricade was set up near your village. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether I understood you properly, but let me ask. Did you personally go down to the road, to the barricade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally did not see with your own eyes any of the events that took place at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anything there. All I know about that barricade was what I learned from others after the event, but personally, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I know how the barricade was put up, but I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, you told us that you got in touch with the TO headquarters in Vitez in order that they might send in reinforcements which they were not able to do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. When the attack was well under way, it wasn't immediately at the beginning, as if we had prepared for it, but once the attack started, we appealed for assistance. However, some of the people from the villages of Vrhovine, Poculica, Preocica came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are villages close to yours; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, according to your knowledge and recollection, is it true that in that locale, the 325th Mountain Brigade of the BH army was stationed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. The 325th Brigade is a brigade of the Bosniak people, as those present know very well, and there were two parts. One unit was in Preocica and another in Kruscica, so that the Lasva Valley, as far as the Bosniak people is concerned, was left without any army of its own. There were some members of that brigade but who had already joined the brigade, and they were stationed at the village of Preocica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, that is precisely what I was asking. In the village of Preocica, at least a part of the 325th Mountain Brigade was stationed, and it was under the command of Sedzanovic [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I was telling you, I was not a member of any military bodies. I participated in civilian affairs. So please don't ask me much about the military organisation because I really don't know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But regardless of that, Mr. K, regardless of the fact that you were not at the barricade, at the roadblock, but you heard about those events. Did you also hear that members of the Bosniak security disarmed four HVO soldiers who came along the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that, but I said in my testimony that the aim was to get weapons, but those weapons were seized from them. So it is possible that that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. K, are you aware that on that occasion, a military policeman from Kiseljak was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there was shooting with incendiary bullets and that some stables of local villagers, Bosniaks, were set on fire. Do you know that some stables owned by Croats in the area were also set on fire, such as, for instance, Drago Josipovic's shed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: It wasn't just stables, but some houses were set on fire as well. As for Josipovic's stable, I didn't pass by that house, but I think it was burnt because in the immediate vicinity was Hasim Ahmic's stable which they missed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but, nevertheless, Josipovic's stable was set on fire. Mr. K, is it true that from Vitez, from the municipality, the president at the time, Mr. Skopljak, came to establish the damage done in your village and that later on, with the financial assistance of the municipality, the damage was repaired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I know that with Mr. Zeco, there were Croat representatives. I wasn't present there to know exactly who was present, but I know that an agreement was reached to compensate the damage and that it was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the damage was repaired, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, allow me now to ask you several questions in connection with the imprisonment of your son. You said that he used to work in the Bratsvo factory, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a military factory, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he was arrested or captured, the exact spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: He was arrested at a place called Stojkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a place within the area of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, in the immediate vicinity of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, as a parent and a father, a worried father, you tried to intervene in favour of your son, you first addressed the commander of the TO staff, Mr. Dzidic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, that was only normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his answer? Did he say that he would try to talk to someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. He wanted to calm me down. Of course, I was upset, and he said, "I'll call," I don't know whom "further up," but nothing came of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after that, you went to see Mr. Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I went to the municipality building and I found him. He received me cordially. We know each other well, and he said, "I am a politician. That is a military matter and I can be of no assistance there."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you first went to see Mr. Dzidic, then Mr. Skopljak, and at the end, you went to see Mr. Cerkez, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. K, what position, when you went to see him, Mr. Cerkez held at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I really -- if I were to say something, I'm afraid I may be wrong. I know that he held a very senior position. I thought that he was head of the military police and that is why I went to ask for his help. However, I later learned that he was in command of the headquarters. But anyway, I don't know what his position was. I went to see him as a friend of mine, as an individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went to see Cerkez because you knew him from before, from Bratsvo, and because you heard that he held a high-ranking position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Mr. Cerkez said that nothing would happen to your son but that he cannot be of assistance, as he was not responsible for what was happening in the area of Novi Travnik, where your son had been arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. He said to me that nothing would happen to him, and he explained why he had been arrested. That was the first time that I heard the word "uhicen" a Croat word used for arrest, and that my son and the other Muslims are being held to be exchanged with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you told us that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Well, that was what he told me. I can't give you a different answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question is, did he also tell you that in view of the fact that your son had been arrested in Novi Travnik, and you came to see him in Vitez, that he was not responsible for the area of Novi Travnik, and that is why he couldn't help you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I don't recollect that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, let me ask you whether you perhaps know. Who was Mr. Cerkez's superior along the chain of military command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: My immediate response would be Blaskic, but I really don't know. I don't know. If I did, I would be glad to give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, I told you at the beginning that I appreciate and feel for you for the tragedy you went through, and that is why I don't wish to ask you in detail about the events of April in Ahmici, but there are some things that I have to ask you nevertheless. Did you see the soldiers who attacked your village, in the sense, did you see which unit it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: That was precisely the problem. The shelling started from a large distance, from Hrasno, Vare, Donja Rovna, et cetera, with heavy artillery. Later, while talking to mothers and women whose sons, fathers, and husbands had been killed, we reconstructed the event and we realised that it was an elaborate tactic because there were one, two, or three HVO soldiers at each Bosniak house, and when the call for prayer came in the morning, they woke people up by calling them by first names, Huso, Mujo, et cetera, and when those people appeared on their front door, they were killed. If they appeared with their wives, the wives were killed as well. As for the unit, I saw soldiers who were running across the fields, but I was unable to identify them. I didn't even dare look anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. K, the soldiers that you did see, were they all dressed in the same uniforms or did they have different kinds of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Possibly, for me, they were all camouflage, and anyway, there were no uniforms such as those worn by the Yugoslav People's Army which one would recognise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. K, tell me, please, did you personally see or hear from someone that Mr. Cerkez was ever in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: In the course of that event? No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. K. The Defence has no further questions, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Sayers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, according to the 1991 census, the total population of Ahmici was 466, with 356 Muslims and 87 Croats. As far as you're aware, is that an accurate figure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1991, Witness K?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: 1991, yes, that is more or less correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I understand that you worked in the Slobodan Princep Seljo factory right up until April the 16th, 1993; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Not right up until the 16th, until the 13th. When my son was arrested, I abandoned my post and didn't go back. I couldn't go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you remember giving a statement to the Centre for Investigating War Crimes and crimes of genocide against Muslims on May the 4th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Let me see. When we reached Zenica, we were approached by all kinds of people from the CSB, the security, journalists, and all kinds of others, and we were telling people everywhere what had happened. Whether I made a statement or not, possibly I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember giving a statement to an investigating judge, Dijana Ajanovic on December the 15th, 1993 as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be fair to say, Witness K, that you've given two statements to the investigators of the Prosecution of this Tribunal, one in February of 1995 and one in August of 1996; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Correct. You have the evidence there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also given testimony in the Kupreskic case, I think we've already established. Do you remember that that was in September of last year, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you sought refuge along with about 150 or 200 residents of Ahmici in the cellar of Mr. Kermo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was pursuant to a civil -- a civilian defence plan drawn up by Mr. Fuad Zeco, the commander of the municipal headquarters for civil defence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco was the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Mr. Zeco was that, but it was us ourselves, the local people, who determined this ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, isn't it true that the October the 19th, 1992 blockade that you spoke about, was actually set up at the Catholic cemetery on the main road to the east of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't get the right interpretation. Not at the cemetery, before the cemetery, looking from the direction of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Isn't it true that the 3rd Corps commander in Zenica ordered the blockade to be erected to prevent HVO units from going towards Travnik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. The 3rd Corps -- or, rather, the commander of the 3rd Corps did not give those orders, but from the local command in Vitez, talking to Fuad, he was told this. Zenica had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just read you a statement from page 1 of your May the 4th, 1993 statement, sir. It says: "First of all, I wish to mention that even before the conflict, we had another one, and the reason for it was the roadblock (ours) set up at the request of the 3rd Corps, which was designed to prevent the HVO units from going towards Travnik." You did give that statement to the Centre for Investigating War Crimes five years ago, six years ago, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I did make a statement, but I think that I didn't say what you have just said, that I never mentioned the 3rd Corps. Because in those days, the 3rd Corps didn't even really exist; it was formed later. So I think that that is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I would just like to have the usher put this on the ELMO. It is a copy of Mr. K's statement of that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the name of the witness appears on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then we ought to put this in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Take it off. If it's given to the witness, he can answer any questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just under the word "Statement," Witness K, is it not true that it says precisely what I just said? Witness K, I understand that you've been through terrible things, and I don't want to make a meal of this, but it does say that in your statement, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. These statements were given in an atmosphere of confusion. It was months, maybe a month -- less than a month after all that evil that happened. I may have identified the corps with something else, but I still claim that this was not right. Even if I said so, it was not right. Because this was a confusing situation. There was sorrow and grief, and we still could hear the shooting in our heads, but let me say again that this is not right, what I said there, even if I am sent to prison for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You won't be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness K, you made the same statement about six months later to investigating judge, Dijana Ajanovic, and with the Trial Chamber's permission, I would like to show, I would like the witness to be shown the statement from the investigators?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I wonder, is it the same point again?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It's pretty much the same point, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder whether there's much point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber has the point. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness K, isn't it a fact that the army of the BiH actually had an organised unit in the village of Ahmici in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I said that it did not have, and I claim with full responsibility that we did not have a unit. We had ourselves organised ourselves as villagers. We were civilians. We ourselves organised some kind of guard duty in the evenings, but this was not an organised unit that could engage in combat with another unit. Of course, we didn't just sit and watch. We tried to find a way out, to defend ourselves, but there was no organised unit in the sense of a military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just, if I may, read your statement to the investigating judge on December the 15th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With the Trial Chamber's permission, I would like to show the witness, or he can consult the original in Croatian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the investigating judge: "I would like to begin my testimony starting with October 1992. At that time, there was an organised unit of the army of BiH in our village." That's what you told the investigating judge six years ago, is it not, sir, on page 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's on page 2, sir, lines 3 through 5 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: We were still called the Territorial Defence. We received orders from the higher command. Here I mentioned the higher command from Vitez. I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you just turn to page 2, sir, would you just read the first few --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Here is page 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go three lines down, and could you just read that into the record, sir, so that the Trial Chamber can get an accurate translation of what you told the investigating judge six years ago? Please read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: You mean the part "We were called the TO," from the beginning? From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the beginning of the passage, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: But let me underline that that was a statement I made then. "I should like to begin my testimony with October 1992. In those days, there was an organised unit in our village of the BH army, but we were called the Territorial Defence." You see, that is a different pair of gloves altogether. The Territorial Defence is a military formation in which both Muslims and Croats participated, and it is true that such units existed. But this was a unit of a civilian nature, a local nature, and representatives of all ethnic groups participated, all ethnic groups living in the area in 1992. This was before the war. And this was a legal obligation. Even women participated, as well as able-bodied men up to the age of 50 or 55; I'm not quite sure. It was a legal obligation to have such units, and that's what the reference is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, could you just read on, the next few lines, please? I think that will help elucidate what you told the investigating judge six years ago.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: Yes. "We were assigned the task to set up a barricade so that HVO units from Kiseljak and Busovaca would be prevented from going to Novi Travnik." Wait a minute. I have to read it all. Here it really does say that a barricade was put up, and it was. The way it was put up is not described here because this is a brief statement. We covered that quickly. I'm not denying that there was no barricade, but what I say is that it was put up by two frustrated policemen, and it did exist. It was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also true, isn't it, and I think you've told the Trial Chamber this, that reinforcements from the local TO headquarters at Preocica and two other towns, Poculica and Vrhovine, arrived to reinforce the organised unit that was present in the village when that barricade was erected; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K
utterances.text: No. It is correct that they did arrive, but there was no organised unit. They came to us, to help us, the common people. All young men who were fit for military service, all our young men went to the brigade, which was deployed in a completely different location, and only the elderly men stayed behind, of my generation, and those who were not fit for military service. And being aware of that situation, they sent to us these men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, it's just after 4.00. How much longer do you anticipate being with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I would think perhaps 30 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Tomorrow morning then. Mr. Lopez-Terres, it may be as well to call the witness tomorrow morning who may take a bit of time and who has to get away, rather than trying to interpose any other witnesses, in order that we make sure that we do finish that witness this week. Perhaps you would like to have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the proper measures will be taken so that it can be done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K, could you be back, please, tomorrow morning at half past nine so that we can complete your evidence then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of September, 1999, at 9:30 a.m. 23 24 25
